scene.testo: They asked him one question. If the bombing of Germany had to be done again, what would have been the better plan? The man who answered had run Hitler's war production. His reply was not a city. It was one small industry.
He also gave them a number. Four months. That, he said, was all it would have taken to bring German war production to a complete collapse. Not years. Not an endless campaign. Four months.

Here is the strange part. The Americans had already attacked that very target. Twice. On the second try, they lost sixty bombers in a single afternoon. And then, for four months, they did not go back.

Albert Speer was an architect before he was anything else. He designed buildings for Hitler. In February 1942, Hitler named him Minister of Armaments. From then on, Germany's tanks, guns and aircraft engines depended on factories he controlled.
Speer was intelligent, organized, and very good at explaining his own point of view. After the war, that last talent mattered most of all. Remember it. It will matter again before this story ends.
When Germany surrendered in May 1945, Speer was still in the north, at Glucksburg, with the last government of Admiral Doenitz. The Allies were closing in. Soon, the interrogators would arrive.

The Americans who came to question him were not soldiers. They were economists and analysts from the United States Strategic Bombing Survey. Among them were Paul Nitze, John Kenneth Galbraith and George Ball.
They wanted to know what the bombing had actually done to Germany. For about a week, Speer answered their questions, day after day. He was polite, precise, and eager to be helpful.

The Survey printed his answer in its report on one German industry. Asked about a better and more effective plan of air attack, Speer replied that the destruction of the ball bearing industry would have been the cheapest way to cripple Germany.

In his own words, as the Survey recorded them, it would have led to a complete collapse of production after four months. In some critical sectors, he added, the effect would have come in as little as two to eight weeks.
scene.q: United States Strategic Bombing Survey report

scene.testo: The target was ball bearings. Small steel balls and rings, the kind of part most people never think about. But without them, almost nothing in a modern army can turn.

They were inside every tank, every truck, every aircraft engine, every gun turret, every submarine. Take away the bearings, and the machines of war stop moving. The Germans knew it. So did the Allies.
When the bombing began, about half of all German ball bearing output came from factories in one city in northern Bavaria. Schweinfurt, and the area around it. One city. One weakness.

Speer understood how exposed this was. In September 1942, he warned Hitler that the Schweinfurt plants were critical to the entire war effort. Hitler ordered more antiaircraft guns for the city. Little else was done.
The Americans had reached the same conclusion. On August 17, 1943, the Eighth Air Force sent about 200 B-17 Flying Fortresses against Schweinfurt. The flight from England was long.
Escort fighters could not fly beyond the German border. Past that point, the bombers were on their own. Thirty-six of them did not return. But the bombs had done their work.

According to the Survey, by September production at Schweinfurt had fallen to 35 percent of its level before the raid. Inside Germany, Speer's people were close to panic. Moving the industry would have halted production for months.

So they repaired the damaged plants where they stood. Army reserve stocks of bearings filled the gap, enough for six to eight weeks. Speer later wrote that bearings were carried from the plants to the assembly lines daily, often in knapsacks.

He remembered the fear of those weeks. We asked ourselves anxiously, he wrote, when the enemy would realize that he could paralyze the output of thousands of armaments plants by destroying just five or six relatively small targets.

The second blow came on October 14, 1943. Speer was at Hitler's headquarters in East Prussia when Goering telephoned with good news. The air defenses, Hitler was told, had won a great victory. The countryside was covered with wrecked American bombers.

Speer was uneasy. He telephoned Schweinfurt himself and, after a long struggle, reached the director of a bearing plant. The factories had been badly hit. Oil baths used in bearing production had set the machine shops on fire.

This time, Speer wrote, 67 percent of the output of the most important sizes was lost. For a moment, the Americans had their hands around the throat of the German war machine. But the price was heavy.
Of 228 bombers sent that day, 62 were lost. Another 138 came home damaged. Each bomber carried a crew of ten young Americans. The crews called that day Black Thursday.
The Survey made the point plainly. Losses of that size could not be sustained. Deep raids into Germany without fighter escort stopped. And Schweinfurt was left alone, for four months.

The Germans used that quiet well. Speer appointed one of his hardest managers, Philipp Kessler, as special commissioner for bearings, with power to take whatever men and materials he needed. Machines were moved out of Schweinfurt into villages and small towns.

Engineers redesigned equipment to use fewer ball bearings, or other types of bearings instead. Speer was honest about what saved them. He wrote that what really saved us was that the enemy, to our astonishment, stopped his attacks on the ball bearing industry.

When the bombers finally returned in late February 1944, they came with long-range P-51 Mustangs. American daylight raids and British night raids struck Schweinfurt, one after another. But the target had changed.

By then, the Survey found, Schweinfurt accounted for only about 60 percent of what it had been in August. The rest had been moved. In April, the campaign against bearing plants was dropped, as bombers turned toward the invasion and oil.

Speer's verdict on that spring was blunt. The Allies, he said, had thrown away a success when it was already in their hands. When they returned to Schweinfurt later that year, most of the machines were already gone.

Yet here is the part Speer's account leaves out. In December 1944, at a meeting of his armaments staff, a German officer summed it up in one sentence: no equipment had stopped because of a shortage of bearings.

The American Survey, after reviewing industry records and questioning its managers, reached the same conclusion. It found no evidence that the attacks on the ball bearing industry had any measurable effect on essential war production.

Even Speer's deputy, Karl Sauer, claimed the industry could have recovered anyway. The Survey called that a hypothesis. So was Speer's. Which answer was right? Speer repeated his view a year later, in June 1946.

The Royal Air Force put the same question to him, and this time he set out the conditions. Strike every bearing plant at once. Repeat the raids every two weeks. Smash every attempt at rebuilding. Four months, if all of that were done.

In 1943, the Allies could not have done it. They lacked the bombers to hit every plant at once, and the fighters to escort them that deep. In the end, they found the target that truly broke Germany. It was oil.

Speer told the Survey that too. But the question at Glucksburg was what could have been done earlier. His answer is still printed in the American report: the cheapest way to stop Hitler's factories was to hit a few small ball bearing plants.

The men who flew to Schweinfurt had tried it, at a cost no air force could keep paying. And for four months, no one went back to finish the job. Speer had given the Americans four months. But in the Ardennes, Hitler's high command needed only four days to learn its last great offensive in the West had failed.

descrizione:
In May 1945, American interrogators asked Albert Speer, Hitler's armaments minister, what better plan of air attack the Allies could have followed. His documented answer: destroy the ball bearing industry, and German production would collapse within four months.

This documentary traces the story from Schweinfurt, the August and October 1943 raids, and Black Thursday, to the German recovery and the Strategic Bombing Survey's verdict. We examine what Speer said, what the records show, and why the lost window mattered.

Based on Allied interrogation reports, Speer's memoirs and the United States Strategic Bombing Survey. Subscribe to WWII Testimony for more accounts from the other side, in their own words.
